###### Abstract

Continual post-training enables foundation models to acquire new
knowledge while preserving existing capabilities. Recent work suggests
that on-policy learning can mitigate forgetting, with on-policy
self-distillation emerging as a particularly attractive approach. In
this work, we revisit this optimistic view through self-distillation
policy optimization (SDPO). Our experiments show that SDPO can
accelerate in-domain specialization when teacher signals are stable and
well aligned, but it struggles to generalize to out-of-distribution
scenarios. In continual post-training, SDPO exhibits stronger forgetting
and can even collapse, whereas on-policy reinforcement learning methods
such as GRPO adapt more conservatively and better preserve prior
capabilities. Further analyses reveal that denser self-distillation
induces larger drift in both parameter space and response space, and can
amplify high-frequency formatting artifacts through a self-reinforcing
teacher–student loop. These findings suggest that on-policy data alone
is insufficient for continual learning. Dense self-distillation can
accelerate specialization when teacher targets are stable and
token-level supervision is reliable, but it should not be treated as a
default stabilizer for continual post-training. Our code is available at
[https://github.com/Moenupa/SDPO-CL](https://github.com/Moenupa/SDPO-CL).

## 1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has emerged as an
effective post-training paradigm for large language models (LLMs)
([Lambert et al., 2024](#bib.bib45); [Guo et al., 2025a](#bib.bib46)).
However, practical systems often require continual post-training across
domains and skills ([Team, 2025](#bib.bib1); [NVIDIA,
2025](#bib.bib43)), raising a significant challenge: models must acquire
new capabilities without forgetting prior ones. Existing work has
suggested an optimistic picture for continual post-training: on-policy
reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) forgets less than supervised fine-tuning
(SFT) ([Lai et al., 2025](#bib.bib44); [Chen et al., 2025](#bib.bib48);
[Shenfeld et al., 2025](#bib.bib41); [Zhang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib40)),
and this benefit has often been attributed to the use of on-policy data
([Chen et al., 2025](#bib.bib48); [Shenfeld et al., 2025](#bib.bib41);
[Zhu et al., 2025](#bib.bib13)).

Recently, on-policy distillation has emerged as an attractive
alternative to sparse reward-based reinforcement learning. By converting
model-generated rollouts into dense token-level supervision, these
methods promise better credit assignment, higher sample efficiency, and
reduced dependence on external teachers or explicit reward models
([Agarwal et al., 2024](#bib.bib19); [Gu et al., 2024](#bib.bib34);
[Thinking Machines Lab, 2025](#bib.bib18)). A particularly appealing
variant is on-policy self-distillation, where the model itself acts as a
teacher by conditioning on demonstrations, feedback, solutions, or other
auxiliary context, and the resulting behavior is distilled back into the
same model. For example, self-distillation fine-tuning (SDFT) uses a
demonstration-conditioned model as its own teacher and demonstrates that
such on-policy distillation can acquire new skills while preserving
prior capabilities ([Shenfeld et al., 2026](#bib.bib29)).
Self-distillation policy optimization (SDPO) similarly uses a
more-informed, feedback-conditioned teacher to provide dense token-level
supervision to the student policy ([Hübotter et al., 2026](#bib.bib15)).
Together, these works suggest that on-policy self-distillation may be a
practical recipe for continual learning, combining the on-policy nature
of RFT that mitigates forgetting with the efficiency of dense supervised
updates for learning new knowledge.

Figure 1: GRPO versus SDPO relative performance to base model (%) across
sequentially learned tasks (1–4) and out-of-distribution (OOD)
benchmarks. The line plots track performance retention across domains
(Math, Science, ToolUse, Coding, and macro OOD average) as new tasks are
acquired. The bar charts break down final relative performance across
specific OOD benchmarks.

However, this view conflates two distinct ingredients: where the data
come from and which objective is used to update the model. On-policy
sampling determines the histories on which the model is trained, but the
training objective determines which continuation distribution is
reinforced at each history. This distinction is especially important for
dense self-distillation. When every token becomes a training target,
teacher drift, noisy rationales, formatting conventions, and
domain-specific artifacts can be reinforced as repeatedly as useful
behavior ([Li et al., 2026](#bib.bib42); [Kim et al.,
2026](#bib.bib47)). Thus, on-policy self-distillation may avoid the
off-policy mismatch of SFT, but it does not automatically inherit the
conservative update bias of sequence-level on-policy RFT.

This paper studies whether on-policy self-distillation enables reliable
continual post-training. We focus on self-distillation policy
optimization (SDPO, [Hübotter et al., 2026](#bib.bib15)) and compare it
with sequence-level reward optimization (GRPO, [Shao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib17)), from two perspectives:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

To answer these questions, we conduct post-training experiments in both
single-domain and multi-domain continual settings. We vary the
supervision density by comparing GRPO, standard SDPO, and SDPO variants
with additional teacher strategies
([Section 3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Token-Level Supervision Requires Fresh but Temporally Stable Teachers ‣ 3 Token-Level Dense Supervision is Powerful but Sensitive ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training"))
or supervision tweaks
([Section 3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 CoT Distillation: More Supervision Is Not Always Better ‣ 3 Token-Level Dense Supervision is Powerful but Sensitive ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")),
and evaluate on in-distribution and general benchmarks to assess
specialization, retention, and transfer
([Sections 4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Rethinking OOD Generalization: Intermediate-Distance Interference ‣ 4 SDPO Trades Retention for Specialization ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")
and [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Continual Learning Exposes the Accumulated Cost of Dense Supervision ‣ 4 SDPO Trades Retention for Specialization ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")).
Finally, we connect behavior to diagnostics—parameter and response drift
([Section 5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Dense Supervision Causes Larger Parameter and Response Drift ‣ 5 Understanding SDPO in Continual Post-training ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")),
collapse modes
([Section 5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Collapse as Artifact Amplification Under Dense Self-Distillation ‣ 5 Understanding SDPO in Continual Post-training ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")),
and theoretical analysis
([Section 5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Theoretical View on Forgetting: Excess KL Drift ‣ 5 Understanding SDPO in Continual Post-training ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training"))
to interpret our observations.

Our results show that on-policy self-distillation offers a powerful yet
fragile training signal
([Figure 1](#S1.F1 "In 1 Introduction ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")).
SDPO can substantially improve performance on the current training
domain, but it also increases the risk of drift, interference, and even
collapse. Our observations suggest that supervision density introduces a
trade-off: it strengthens the local learning signal, but also increases
sensitivity, domain mismatch, and accumulated artifacts. Our main
contributions are:

- •
  We separate two factors often conflated in continual post-training:
  on-policy data and the objective used to turn on-policy rollouts into
  updates. This lets us ask whether on-policy self-distillation inherits
  the retention benefits attributed to on-policy RL.
- •
  We show that SDPO is a strong specialization method but a fragile
  continual-learning signal. Its benefits depend on teacher stability
  and token reliability; CoT and fast teacher updates can amplify noise
  and artifacts.
- •
  Across single-domain and staged continual post-training, SDPO exhibits
  weaker retention than GRPO, with forgetting concentrated on
  neighboring-yet-misaligned tasks and accumulating across domains.
- •
  Parameter drift, response drift, collapse analysis, and an excess-KL
  view diagnose how and why SDPO yields such forgetting behavior.

## 2 Preliminaries

### 2.1 Post-Training of Large Language Models

#### Reinforcement Learning for Post-Training.

Reinforcement learning is widely used to post-train large language
models with preference signals or reward functions derived from human
feedback, automated evaluators, or verifiable correctness criteria
([Stiennon et al., 2020](#bib.bib23); [Ouyang et al., 2022](#bib.bib20);
[Ziegler et al., 2019](#bib.bib21); [Bai et al., 2022](#bib.bib22)).
Recent methods, such as direct preference optimization ([Rafailov et
al., 2023](#bib.bib26)), recast preference optimization as a supervised
objective, while on-policy algorithms like group relative policy
optimization ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib17)) optimize relative
advantages over sampled response groups, often improving stability and
scalability in large-scale settings.

#### On-Policy Distillation.

On-policy distillation (OPD) methods construct training targets from
samples generated by the current policy or its improved variants,
thereby converting reinforcement signals into supervised learning
updates ([Agarwal et al., 2024](#bib.bib19); [Gu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib34)). Recent self-distillation methods remove the need for
a separate teacher by running the same model under different information
conditions: the student observes only the original prompt, while the
teacher is augmented with privileged context $`c`$. The privileged
signal can come from demonstrations or examples ([Snell et al.,
2022](#bib.bib28); [Shenfeld et al., 2026](#bib.bib29)), correct
solutions or textual feedback ([Hübotter et al., 2026](#bib.bib15)), or
revision contexts, hints, and task-level feedback transformations ([Zhao
et al., 2026](#bib.bib30); [Ye et al., 2026](#bib.bib31)).

#### Chain-of-Thought Reasoning.

Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting and training encourage LLMs to generate
intermediate reasoning before final answers, often improving performance
on arithmetic, symbolic, and commonsense tasks ([Wei et al.,
2022](#bib.bib24); [Kojima et al., 2022](#bib.bib25)). Under
final-answer supervision, this lengthens the credit-assignment horizon;
with step-level or process rewards, it offers denser feedback and
improves interpretability ([Uesato et al., 2022](#bib.bib32); [Lightman
et al., 2023](#bib.bib11)). CoT also has drawbacks: it increases
inference cost, may propagate errors across steps, and the generated
rationales need not faithfully reflect the model’s actual decision
process ([Turpin et al., 2023](#bib.bib33)).

#### Continual Post-Training.

Continual learning ([Guo et al., 2025b](#bib.bib39)) studies how models
incorporate new knowledge without catastrophic forgetting of acquired
ones. Common approaches use regularization, replay, or reference-model
constraints to mitigate catastrophic forgetting across training stages
([Kirkpatrick et al., 2017](#bib.bib27); [Zhu et al., 2021](#bib.bib38);
[Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib37)). A growing line of work shows that RFT
can substantially mitigate forgetting in continual post-training ([Lai
et al., 2025](#bib.bib44); [Shenfeld et al., 2025](#bib.bib41); [Chen et
al., 2025](#bib.bib48)). For example, [Lai et al. (2025)](#bib.bib44)
find that this benefit is not mainly due to explicit KL penalties or
chain-of-thought prompting, but rather to the implicit regularization
induced by reward-guided policy updates. Complementarily, [Shenfeld et
al. (2025)](#bib.bib41) argue that online RL is biased toward KL-minimal
solutions among the policies that solve a new task, thereby reducing the
distributional shift from the base model that is predictive of
forgetting. Similarly, [Chen et al. (2025)](#bib.bib48) identify the use
of on-policy data as a key factor behind RL’s robustness.

### 2.2 Group Relative Policy Optimization

Group relative policy optimization (GRPO, [Shao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib17)) assigns rewards at the sequence level. Given a prompt
$`x\sim\mathcal{D}`$, GRPO samples a group of $`G`$ responses
$`\{y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}`$ from the current policy, i.e.,
$`y_{i}\sim\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(\cdot\mid x)`$, evaluates each
response with a reward model to obtain rewards $`\{r_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}`$,
and computes group-relative advantages by normalizing rewards within the
group, e.g.,
$`A_{i}=(r_{i}-\mathrm{mean}(\{r_{j}\}_{j=1}^{G}))/(\mathrm{std}(\{r_{j}\}_{j=1}^{G})+\epsilon)`$.
Training optimizes a PPO-style clipped objective:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}(\theta)=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\frac{1}{|y_{i}|}\sum_{t=1}^{|y_{i}|}\min\bigl(\rho_{i,t}A_{i},\mathrm{clip}(\rho_{i,t},1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon)A_{i}\bigr)-\lambda D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\parallel\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid x)\bigr),
``` |  |

where
$`\rho_{i,t}=\nicefrac{{\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,t}\mid x,y_{i,<t})}}{{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(y_{i,t}\mid x,y_{i,<t})}}`$
and $`\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}`$ is a reference policy used for KL
regularization. In essence, GRPO is a critic-free policy optimization
method that stabilizes reinforcement learning by using relative rewards
among multiple sampled responses to the same prompt.

### 2.3 On-Policy Self-Distillation

Self-distillation policy optimization (SDPO, [Hübotter et al.,
2026](#bib.bib15)) instead provides dense token-level rewards using the
same model as both teacher and student. For each student-generated
response $`y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)`$, the student is trained to
align with the more-informed teacher $`\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,c)`$
having richer context $`c`$ (including solutions or other auxiliary
signals). Training minimizes the generalized Jensen–Shannon divergence
(JSD,
[Equation A.2](#A1.E2 "In Generalized Jensen–Shannon (JS) divergence. ‣ Appendix A Math Notations ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training"))
between student and teacher distributions:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SDPO}}(\theta)=\sum_{t}D_{\mathrm{JSD}}(\beta)\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})\parallel\mathrm{stopgrad}\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,c,y_{<t})\right)\right).
``` |  |

This yields dense supervision: instead of a single reward for the whole
sequence, SDPO encourages student distribution at each generated token
to align with more informed teacher distribution.

(a) Performance ranking across six benchmarks after Math, ToolUse, and
Science training.

(b) Training dynamics on Math-SDPO with different teacher EMAs
$`\alpha\in\{0,0.5\%,1\%,2\%,5\%\}`$.

Figure 2: Effect of SDPO teacher EMA update rate $`\alpha`$. No single
$`\alpha`$ is globally optimal. (a) Ranking-based radar plots. A larger

## 3 Token-Level Dense Supervision is Powerful but Sensitive

First, we claim that SDPO’s benefits depend on the quality of the dense
signal. SDPO distills token logits from the teacher model, improving
sample efficiency because every generated token contributes supervision.
However, it also means that teacher noise, temporal mismatch, and
formatting artifacts are reinforced many times within a single response.
We therefore begin by asking: *how do token-level reward stability
([Section 3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Token-Level Supervision Requires Fresh but Temporally Stable Teachers ‣ 3 Token-Level Dense Supervision is Powerful but Sensitive ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training"))
and density
([Section 3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 CoT Distillation: More Supervision Is Not Always Better ‣ 3 Token-Level Dense Supervision is Powerful but Sensitive ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training"))
affect self-distillation?*

### 3.1 Token-Level Supervision Requires Fresh but Temporally Stable Teachers

A natural intuition in SDPO is that the teacher should be updated
frequently: a fresher teacher should better reflect the student’s latest
improvements and therefore provide stronger token-level supervision. To
test this intuition, we sweep the EMA update rate
$`\alpha\in\{0,0.5\%,1\%,2\%,5\%\}`$:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Theta_{\text{teacher}}^{(k)}=(1-\alpha)\Theta_{\text{teacher}}^{(k-1)}+\alpha\Theta_{\text{student}}^{(k)}.
``` |  |

Surprisingly, freshness alone does not predict performance. As shown in
[Figure 2(a)](#S2.F2.sf1 "In Figure 2 ‣ 2.3 On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ 2 Preliminaries ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training"),
no single $`\alpha`$ is uniformly optimal: in Math-SDPO, $`\alpha=1\%`$
gives the best overall profile, while $`\alpha=5\%`$ performs worst; in
ToolUse training, the frozen teacher is best, although $`\alpha=5\%`$ is
competitive. This raises a question: *if a larger EMA rate makes the
teacher fresher, why can it hurt SDPO so severely?*

We argue that EMA entangles two different properties of the teacher:
*freshness* and *temporal stability*. A larger $`\alpha`$ makes the
teacher weights closer to the current student, but it also makes the
teacher a more rapidly moving target. This is particularly risky for
dense distillation: because SDPO applies supervision at every generated
token, small teacher fluctuations can be reinforced repeatedly within a
single response. The training curves in
[Figure 2(b)](#S2.F2.sf2 "In Figure 2 ‣ 2.3 On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ 2 Preliminaries ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")
support this view. Large EMA rates, especially $`\alpha=2\%`$ and
$`\alpha=5\%`$, observe late-stage increases in entropy and JS
divergence, indicating growing teacher–student mismatch and less
reliable token targets. Smaller or frozen teachers avoid this
instability, but they introduce the opposite problem: the teacher can
become stale and provide a weakening optimization signal as the student
evolves.

To separate freshness from per-step teacher dynamics, we introduce a
simple *restart-and-freeze* strategy named StableSDPO. Instead of
updating the teacher continuously, we periodically refresh it from the
current student and then keep it frozen within the next interval:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Theta_{\text{teacher}}\leftarrow(1-\gamma)\Theta_{\text{teacher}}^{\text{old}}+\gamma\Theta_{\text{student}}^{(k)},\quad 0<\gamma\leq 1.
``` |  |

This design preserves teacher freshness at refresh points while removing
the step-to-step volatility of EMA updates. For comparison with EMA, we
match the effective $`k`$-step refresh amount by
$`\gamma\approx 1-(1-\alpha)^{k}`$; for example, $`\alpha=5\%`$ over
$`k=10`$ steps corresponds to $`\gamma\approx 0.40`$.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Teacher Strategy | AIME | Math500 | GPQA | ZLogic | MMLU-R | Avg |
| – | 32.71 | 73.85 | 62.94 | 81.62 | 86.02 | 67.43 |
| SDPO (EMA $`\alpha=0`$) | 56.42 | 84.29 | 58.72 | 74.50 | 85.47 | 71.88 |
| StableSDPO ($`\gamma=1`$) | 57.50 | 85.05 | 60.86 | 74.68 | 86.60 | 72.94$`\uparrow`$1.06 |
| SDPO (EMA $`\alpha=5\%`$) | 34.38 | 78.97 | 55.87 | 73.68 | 83.82 | 65.34 |
| StableSDPO ($`\gamma=40\%`$) | 55.00 | 84.62 | 59.03 | 73.50 | 87.05 | 71.84$`\uparrow`$6.50 |

Table 1: Math-SDPO performance (Acc@8). Restart-and-freeze offers a
middle ground: it periodically re-initializes the teacher but prevents
per-step noise from being distilled repeatedly.

Figure 3: Training dynamics during Math-SDPO with teacher frozen versus
10-step-hard-restart.

The results in
[Table 1](#S3.T1 "In 3.1 Token-Level Supervision Requires Fresh but Temporally Stable Teachers ‣ 3 Token-Level Dense Supervision is Powerful but Sensitive ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")
strongly support this decomposition. Replacing continuous EMA with
matched restart-and-freeze substantially repairs the destructive
behavior of $`\alpha=5\%`$: on AIME, performance improves from 34.38% to
55.00%, and the average score improves from 65.34% to 71.84%, a gain of
6.50 points. Importantly, StableSDPO also improves over the frozen
teacher: hard restart with $`\gamma=1`$ outperforms the frozen teacher
on all five benchmarks, improving the average score from 71.88% to
72.94%. Thus, the problem is not that freshness is harmful. Rather,
freshness is useful only when it is delivered through a stable teacher
signal. The training dynamics in
[Figure 3](#S3.F3 "In 3.1 Token-Level Supervision Requires Fresh but Temporally Stable Teachers ‣ 3 Token-Level Dense Supervision is Powerful but Sensitive ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")
further illustrate this point. The frozen teacher produces smooth
curves, but its entropy and JS divergence gradually decline, suggesting
that the teacher becomes increasingly outdated. In contrast,
restart-and-freeze produces bounded oscillations aligned with refresh
events: each restart renews the teacher signal, and avoids noisy
per-step target changes. The JS divergence remains bounded, with neither
late-stage blow-up nor collapse.

### 3.2 CoT Distillation: More Supervision Is Not Always Better

We next consider the supervision density of SDPO, by additionally
distilling Chain-of-Thought tokens. This is a stronger test of the
dense-supervision hypothesis: if more token-level targets were uniformly
beneficial, CoT distillation should consistently improve performance.
[Figure 4(a)](#S3.F4.sf1 "In Figure 4 ‣ 3.2 CoT Distillation: More Supervision Is Not Always Better ‣ 3 Token-Level Dense Supervision is Powerful but Sensitive ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")
shows the opposite: CoT helps ToolUse training but hurts Math and
Science training.

We attribute this contrast to the reliability of intermediate tokens.
CoT distillation does not merely add more supervision; it changes the
target from answer-producing behavior to a particular reasoning
trajectory. In long-form Math and Science tasks, such trajectories are
underdetermined and often contain redundant self-checks, uncertain
interpretations, formatting habits, or incorrect intermediate claims.
These tokens are weakly tied to final correctness, so distilling them
can dilute credit assignment and encourage imitation of reasoning
artifacts. This is reflected in Math training by longer responses,
higher entropy, and larger JS divergence
([Figure 4(b)](#S3.F4.sf2 "In Figure 4 ‣ 3.2 CoT Distillation: More Supervision Is Not Always Better ‣ 3 Token-Level Dense Supervision is Powerful but Sensitive ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")).

By contrast, ToolUse traces are short and schema-constrained. CoT
therefore acts as useful process supervision in ToolUse training,
yielding stable dynamics and improved BFCLv4 performance
([Figure 4(c)](#S3.F4.sf3 "In Figure 4 ‣ 3.2 CoT Distillation: More Supervision Is Not Always Better ‣ 3 Token-Level Dense Supervision is Powerful but Sensitive ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")).
Additional EMA ablations further show that long-CoT supervision becomes
especially harmful when the teacher is updated rapidly
([Table D.2](#A4.T2 "In Appendix D Supplementary Results ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")),
consistent with a confirmation-bias loop in which noisy reasoning
patterns are copied into the teacher and reinforced again.

## 4 SDPO Trades Retention for Specialization

The previous section reveals that SDPO’s dense signal is conditional: it
helps only when the teacher is stable and the distilled tokens are
reliable. We now ask whether these local benefits translate into broader
training advantages. *Does token supervision improves
out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization
([Section 4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Rethinking OOD Generalization: Intermediate-Distance Interference ‣ 4 SDPO Trades Retention for Specialization ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")),
and mitigates forgetting in continual post-training
([Section 4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Continual Learning Exposes the Accumulated Cost of Dense Supervision ‣ 4 SDPO Trades Retention for Specialization ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training"))?*

### 4.1 Rethinking OOD Generalization: Intermediate-Distance Interference

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | Math |  | Science |  | ToolUse |  | Coding |  | Logic | Know. |
|  | Method | AIME | Math500 | Science | GPQA | ToolUse | BFCLv4 | Coding | LCBv6 | ZLogic | MMLU-R |

SDPO’s main advantage is specialization, not uniformly better
generalization
([Table 2](#S4.T2 "In 4.1 Rethinking OOD Generalization: Intermediate-Distance Interference ‣ 4 SDPO Trades Retention for Specialization ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")).
Under Math training, $`\text{SDPO}_{0}`$ is the strongest math
specialist, raising AIME from 32.71% to 56.42% and Math500 from 73.85%
to 84.29%. Similarly, Coding-$`\text{SDPO}_{0}`$ improves LCBv6 by
13.39%. These results confirm that token-level supervision can strongly
exploit source-like evaluation distributions.

However, this specialization does not translate into uniform retention.
We decompose relative performance change into positive gain and negative
forgetting
([Equations A.5](#A1.E5 "In Performance Change. ‣ Appendix A Math Notations ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")
and [A.6](#A1.E6 "Equation A.6 ‣ Performance Change. ‣ Appendix A Math Notations ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")),
and demonstrate that the SDPO-induced forgetting pattern is
non-monotonic, as
[Figure 5](#S4.F5 "In 4.1 Rethinking OOD Generalization: Intermediate-Distance Interference ‣ 4 SDPO Trades Retention for Specialization ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")
plots gain and forgetting against the distributional distance measured
by Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD, [Gretton et al., 2012](#bib.bib16)).
Source-like tasks (e.g., $`\textrm{MMD}\lesssim 0.05`$) and very distant
tasks (e.g., $`\textrm{MMD}\gtrsim 0.4`$) mostly improve, while the
largest drops concentrate in intermediate-distance tasks.

GPQA is the clearest intermediate-forget example: it is not the farthest
benchmark, but consistently degrades after SDPO training from multiple
source domains. We interpret this pattern as evidence that GPQA may lie
in an interference region: it is close enough to be affected by
source-domain updates, yet insufficiently aligned to benefit from them.
More broadly, we observe SDPO degradation on Math-to-Science,
Math-to-ZLogic, and Science-to-BFCLv4 (more cases are in
[Table D.4](#A4.T4 "In Appendix D Supplementary Results ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")).

These results suggest that SDPO’s OOD failures are consistent with an
intermediate-distance interference pattern, rather than a simple
monotonic function of distributional distance. Distillation specializes
the model toward the source-domain response manifold. When an OOD task
is very close, this specialization transfers. When it is very far, the
perturbation may not strongly affect it. The most vulnerable tasks are
partially aligned OOD tasks: close enough to be changed, but misaligned
enough not to benefit. This non-monotonic pattern is consistent with
prior theory of continual learning with linear models ([Lin et al.,
2023](#bib.bib36); [Goldfarb et al., 2024](#bib.bib35)), and our results
show that a similar interference regime emerges in LLM continual
post-training,

Table 3: Continual learning performance (Acc@8) of SDPO versus GRPO.
SDPO often wins early (better current-stage), but GRPO wins over time
(better last-stage).

Single-domain interference becomes more severe when updates are composed
across domains. We therefore train models sequentially on Math
$`\rightarrow`$ Science $`\rightarrow`$ ToolUse $`\rightarrow`$ Coding
and evaluate after each stage. We report both *Current*, i.e.,
performance on the current domain immediately after training it, and
*Last*, i.e., performance after the full training sequence.

The continual setting reverses the single-domain picture.
$`\text{SDPO}_{0}`$ is a strong early specializer: it reaches 56.42% on
Math and 65.70% on Science, exceeding GRPO’s 44.67% and 56.39%. However,
these gains do not survive later domain shifts: after the full sequence,
$`\text{SDPO}_{0}`$ drops to 34.38% on Math and 9.93% on ToolUse, and
also falls below the base model on Logic and Knowledge.
$`\text{SDPO}_{0}^{\text{CoT}}`$ degrades even earlier, consistent with
the instability of long-CoT token targets. The most severe case is
$`\text{SDPO}_{5\%}`$, which collapses after the third stage and remains
near zero. By contrast, GRPO adapts more conservatively but retains
capabilities more reliably, achieving final improvements over the base
model across all evaluated categories
([Figures 6](#S4.F6 "In 4.2 Continual Learning Exposes the Accumulated Cost of Dense Supervision ‣ 4 SDPO Trades Retention for Specialization ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")
and [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.2 Continual Learning Exposes the Accumulated Cost of Dense Supervision ‣ 4 SDPO Trades Retention for Specialization ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")).

These results argue that single-domain specialization is not evidence of
continual learning. SDPO’s dense token-level updates can accelerate
local adaptation, but the same updates also accumulate drift,
interference, and artifacts across domain shifts. Sequence-level GRPO is
less aggressive, but its more selective reward signal better supports
long-horizon retention.

## 5 Understanding SDPO in Continual Post-training

### 5.1 Dense Supervision Causes Larger Parameter and Response Drift

The benchmarks report that SDPO adapts more aggressively than GRPO. To
understand why, we look inside the model and ask whether SDPO’s greater
behavioral changes correspond to larger parameter shifts. For each LLM
weight matrix (e.g., self-attention $`V`$) at training step $`k`$:
$`{\mathbf{W}}^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}`$, we compute the compact
singular value decomposition:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
{\mathbf{W}}^{(k)}={\mathbf{U}}^{(k)}{\mathbf{\Sigma}}^{(k)}{{\mathbf{V}}^{(k)}}^{\top},
``` |  |

where $`{\mathbf{U}}^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}`$,
$`{\mathbf{V}}^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}`$, and $`d=\min(m,n)`$.
The SVD decomposes each matrix into input-output directions and their
associated spectral strengths, and we use it to quantify how training
changes the geometry, spectral magnitude, subspace orientation, and
dominant parameter regions of the model. Specifically, we calculate the
following metrics between $`{\mathbf{W}}^{(0)}`$ and
$`{\mathbf{W}}^{(k)}`$:

- •
  *Normalized spectral shift*: $`\ell_{2}`$-normalized drift of the
  singular-value profile in
  [Equation A.8](#A1.E8 "In Normalized spectral shift. ‣ Appendix A Math Notations ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training").
  Larger values indicate substantial strength changes in dominant
  directions.
- •
  *Principal-angle rotation*: maximum rotation within top-$`k`$ left
  singular subspaces, as shown in
  [Equation A.11](#A1.E11 "In Maximum principal-angle rotation. ‣ Appendix A Math Notations ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training").
  A small value implies better preservation of dominant subspaces.
- •
  *Principal-mask overlap*: intersection-over-union of principal masks
  before and after training per
  [Equation A.12](#A1.E12 "In Principal-mask overlap. ‣ Appendix A Math Notations ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training").
  High values mean dominant entries remain important.
- •
  *Principal-mask update sparsity*: intersection-over-union of the
  initial principal mask and the changed-parameter mask in
  [Equation A.14](#A1.E14 "In Principal-mask update sparsity. ‣ Appendix A Math Notations ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training").
  A high value demonstrates that training directly modifies structurally
  important parameters.

(b) Self-Attention $`V`$ shift during continual learning.

(c) AIME embedding shift during Math training, $`x`$-axis denote

[Figures 7(a)](#S5.F7.sf1 "In Figure 7 ‣ 5.1 Dense Supervision Causes Larger Parameter and Response Drift ‣ 5 Understanding SDPO in Continual Post-training ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")
and [7(b)](#S5.F7.sf2 "Figure 7(b) ‣ Figure 7 ‣ 5.1 Dense Supervision Causes Larger Parameter and Response Drift ‣ 5 Understanding SDPO in Continual Post-training ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")
highlight a consistent drift hierarchy. GRPO changes the model least:
its spectral shift and subspace rotation remain small, and its
principal-mask overlap stays near $`99.9\%`$. SDPO variants move
farther, with $`\text{SDPO}_{0}^{\text{CoT}}`$ producing the largest
subspace change. This pattern supports an accumulated-drift explanation
of continual-learning failure: SDPO produces notably larger spectral
shifts and more principal-parameter modifications than GRPO. The
ordering
$`\text{SDPO}_{0}^{\text{CoT}}>\text{SDPO}_{5\%}>\text{SDPO}_{0}>\text{GRPO}`$
matches the aggressiveness of the supervision signal: CoT increases
token coverage, while fast EMA increases target non-stationarity. This
supports the view that denser or less stable token-level targets drive
stronger internal updates.

Parameter drift is mirrored in the model’s outputs. Response-embedding
similarities remain tightly concentrated under GRPO, whereas SDPO shifts
the distribution downward and develops heavier lower tails
([Figures 7(c)](#S5.F7.sf3 "In Figure 7 ‣ 5.1 Dense Supervision Causes Larger Parameter and Response Drift ‣ 5 Understanding SDPO in Continual Post-training ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")
and [7(d)](#S5.F7.sf4 "Figure 7(d) ‣ Figure 7 ‣ 5.1 Dense Supervision Causes Larger Parameter and Response Drift ‣ 5 Understanding SDPO in Continual Post-training ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training"),
embedding computed by Qwen3-Embedding-4B, [Zhang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib14)). This suggests that SDPO does not merely improve
selected answers; it reshapes the response manifold more strongly than
sequence-level GRPO.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### 5.2 Collapse as Artifact Amplification Under Dense Self-Distillation

Finally, we diagnose one extreme failure mode as a case of artifact
amplification in self-distillation. $`\text{SDPO}_{5\%}`$ collapses with
a visible generation artifact: endlessly repeated “\boxed” tokens. This
behavior coincides with a change in final-answer formatting requirement
at the third stage, where ToolUse differs from earlier Math and Science
stages (data samples in
[Section C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Data Samples ‣ Appendix C Training Details ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")).
The collapsed model is over-amplifying the high-frequency pattern from
earlier on-policy training stages, as JS divergence
([Figure 8](#S5.F8 "In 5.2 Collapse as Artifact Amplification Under Dense Self-Distillation ‣ 5 Understanding SDPO in Continual Post-training ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training"))
plummets in the third stage, even to zero within the first few steps of
ToolUse training. More experiments show that reordering data or masking
tokens only partially mitigates this collapse
([Tables D.6](#A4.T6 "In Appendix D Supplementary Results ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")
and [D.5](#A4.T5 "Table D.5 ‣ Appendix D Supplementary Results ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")).

Figure 8: JS divergence during continual-$`\text{SDPO}_{5\%}`$ with
ToolUse or Coding as third stage.

This failure is consistent with the central diagnostic observed
throughout our analyses. Because supervision is token-level, frequent
tokens (e.g., formatting patterns) can receive repeated reinforcement.
As the teacher is derived from the student, such artifacts can enter a
feedback loop we call *confirmation bias*: the student emits the
artifact, the teacher assigns it token-level support, and the next
student update makes the artifact more likely. A frequently refreshed
teacher or denser supervision can worsen this process and, in severe
cases, lead to near-complete collapse.

### 5.3 Theoretical View on Forgetting: Excess KL Drift

Existing studies have revealed that on-policy RL is biased toward
solutions that solve the new task while staying close to the base policy
in KL ([Shenfeld et al., 2025](#bib.bib41)). However, SDPO does not
inherit this bias: its rollouts are on-policy, but its local target is a
teacher distribution conditioned on augmented context, rather than the
KL-minimal distribution induced by a sequence-level reward.

Let $`x\sim\mathcal{D}`$ be a prompt, $`y`$ a response, and
$`S_{x}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}`$ the set of successful responses under a
binary sequence reward. Let $`P_{0}(\cdot\mid x)`$ be the sequence
distribution induced by the base policy $`\pi_{0}`$. For any success
level $`\alpha\in(0,1)`$, define the matched-success Razor policy

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
Q_{\alpha,x}^{\dagger}:=\argmin_{Q:\,Q(S_{x})=\alpha}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl(Q\parallel P_{0}(\cdot\mid x)\bigr).
``` |  | (1) |

Let $`q_{\alpha,x}^{\dagger}(\cdot\mid h_{t})`$ be its autoregressive
token kernel at history $`h_{t}=(x,y_{<t})`$. This is the token
distribution induced by the sequence-level reward: it preserves the base
policy except for the reweighting needed to change the probability of
eventual success. In the exact-success limit $`\alpha\to 1`$,
$`Q_{\alpha,x}^{\dagger}`$ becomes the base-conditioned solution
$`P_{0}(\cdot\mid x,y\in S_{x})`$.

In contrast, SDPO distills a teacher that observes augmented context
$`c`$, such as a solution, rationale, or auxiliary signal. Its local
target is $`T_{c}(\cdot\mid h_{t})=\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid x,c,y_{<t})`$. For
a strict distillation divergence $`D`$, e.g., generalized JSD, the
population token-level target is the teacher projection

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
B(\cdot\mid h_{t})\in\argmin_{u\in\Delta(\mathcal{V})}\mathbb{E}_{c\mid h_{t}}D\bigl(u,T_{c}(\cdot\mid h_{t})\bigr).
``` |  | (2) |

When $`c`$ is deterministic, this reduces to
$`B(\cdot\mid h_{t})=T_{c}(\cdot\mid h_{t})`$. Let
$`P_{B}(\cdot\mid x)`$ be the sequence distribution induced by this SDPO
token target and set $`\alpha_{x}=P_{B}(S_{x}\mid x)`$.

###### Theorem 1 (Teacher projection induces excess KL drift).

Assume $`0<\alpha_{x}<1`$. Then

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl(P_{B}(\cdot\mid x)\parallel P_{0}(\cdot\mid x)\bigr)-D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl(Q_{\alpha_{x},x}^{\dagger}\parallel P_{0}(\cdot\mid x)\bigr)`$ |  | (3) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim P_{B}(\cdot\mid x)}\sum_{t=1}^{|y|}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl(B(\cdot\mid h_{t})\parallel q_{\alpha_{x},x}^{\dagger}(\cdot\mid h_{t})\bigr)\geq 0.`$ |  |  |

The inequality is strict whenever the SDPO teacher target differs from
the sequence-reward Razor kernel on a set of histories with positive
$`P_{B}`$-probability.

The no-excess-drift case is therefore restrictive: SDPO must satisfy
$`B(\cdot\mid h_{t})=q_{\alpha_{x},x}^{\dagger}(\cdot\mid h_{t})`$ at
every visited history. This is not implied by teacher–student parameter
sharing. Because the teacher conditions on augmented context $`c`$, it
may select a particular reasoning trace, formatting pattern, or artifact
even when many continuations are equally successful. Thus, SDPO’s
on-policy sampling controls where supervision is applied, but the
distribution selected at each token is the teacher projection, not the
KL-minimal sequence-reward projection. Combined with the KL-forgetting
law, the excess drift in
[Equation 3](#S5.E3 "In Theorem 1 (Teacher projection induces excess KL drift). ‣ 5.3 Theoretical View on Forgetting: Excess KL Drift ‣ 5 Understanding SDPO in Continual Post-training ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")
predicts additional forgetting. Full proofs are in
[Appendix B](#A2 "Appendix B Proofs ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training").

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## 6 Conclusion

This paper studied whether on-policy self-distillation improves
continual post-training. Our results indicate that SDPO can be an
effective specialization method when teacher signals are stable and
aligned with the target domain. However, it is not uniformly beneficial
for continual learning. SDPO’s token supervision amplifies both useful
supervision and harmful artifacts, making it sensitive to teacher
quality, update schedules, and token structure. Compared with GRPO, SDPO
variants exhibit greater forgetting, instability, parameter drift, and
response-manifold shifts.

The main lesson is not that on-policy self-distillation methods are
ineffective, but they are not automatically safe. Token supervision can
be a rapid specialization signal, but also a potentially dangerous
signal: each token can reinforce useful signals and harmful artifacts.
Sequence-level methods such as GRPO learn more slowly, but in our
experiments, they preserve capabilities more reliably. Thus, the future
of on-policy self-distillation for continual learning likely depends not
on making the signal denser, but on safeguarding it through token
weighting, teacher controls, or data balancing strategies to be more
selective, stable, and artifact-aware.

## Appendix A Math Notations

#### Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence.

For two discrete distributions $`P(\mathcal{X})`$ and
$`Q(\mathcal{X})`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\parallel Q)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}P(x)\log\!\left(\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}\right).
``` |  | (A.1) |

#### Generalized Jensen–Shannon (JS) divergence.

A weighted average of two KL divergences from $`P`$ and $`Q`$ to their
mixture with $`\beta\in(0,1)`$ ($`\beta=0.5`$ recovers the standard
symmetric JS divergence):

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
D_{\mathrm{JSD}}(\beta)(P\parallel Q)=\beta{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\parallel\beta P+(1-\beta)Q)}+(1-\beta)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\parallel\beta P+(1-\beta)Q).
``` |  | (A.2) |

#### Performance Change.

We measure absolute ($`\Delta`$) and relative ($`\delta`$) change
against the base model:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\Delta_{m,\mathrm{train},\mathrm{eval}}={P_{m,\mathrm{train},\mathrm{eval}}}-{P_{\mathrm{base},\mathrm{eval}}},`$ |  | (A.3) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\delta_{m,\mathrm{train},\mathrm{eval}}=\nicefrac{{\Delta_{m,\mathrm{train},\mathrm{eval}}}}{{P_{\mathrm{base},\mathrm{eval}}}}\times 100\%,`$ |  | (A.4) |

where $`m`$ is the training method, $`\mathrm{train}`$ is the training
domain, and $`\mathrm{eval}`$ is the evaluation benchmark. We define
*gain* $`G`$ and *forgetting* $`F`$ as the positive and negative part of
the relative change:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle G_{m,\mathrm{train},\mathrm{eval}}=\max(0,\delta_{m,\mathrm{train},\mathrm{eval}}),`$ |  | (A.5) |
|  | $`\displaystyle F_{m,\mathrm{train},\mathrm{eval}}=\max(0,-\delta_{m,\mathrm{train},\mathrm{eval}}).`$ |  | (A.6) |

#### Intersection-over-Union.

For two masks $`A`$ and $`B`$ (e.g., predicted mask and ground-truth
mask),

|     |                                                |     |       |
|-----|------------------------------------------------|-----|-------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \IoU(A,B)=\nicefrac{{|A\cap B|}}{{|A\cup B|}},
       ```                                             |     | (A.7) |

where $`|\cdot|`$ denotes cardinality. The quantity lies in $`[0,1]`$,
with $`1`$ for a perfect overlap.

#### Normalized spectral shift.

It is defined as the $`\ell_{2}`$-normalized drift of the singular-value
profile:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{NSS}\left({\mathbf{W}}^{(0)},{\mathbf{W}}^{(k)}\right)=\tfrac{\left\lVert\sigma\!\left({\mathbf{W}}^{(0)}\right)-\sigma\!\left({\mathbf{W}}^{(k)}\right)\right\rVert_{2}}{\left\lVert\sigma\!\left({\mathbf{W}}^{(0)}\right)\right\rVert_{2}}.
``` |  | (A.8) |

#### Principal-mask (PM) and Principal-angles (PAs).

Given
$`{\mathbf{W}}^{(k)}_{r}={\mathbf{U}}^{(k)}_{r}{\mathbf{\Sigma}}^{(k)}_{r}{{\mathbf{V}}^{(k)}_{r}}^{\top}`$
as the rank-$`r`$ approximation, PM is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
{\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{principal}}}^{(k)}[i,j]=\mathbb{I}\left(\left|{\mathbf{W}}^{(k)}_{r}[i,j]\right|\geq{\tau}^{(k)}_{\eta}\right),
``` |  | (A.9) |

where $`{\tau}^{(k)}_{\eta}`$ is a threshold controlled by the
hyperparameter $`\eta`$. Principal angles are

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\theta_{i}({\mathbf{W}}^{(0)},{\mathbf{W}}^{(k)})=\arccos\sigma_{i}\left({{\mathbf{U}}^{(0)}_{r}}^{\top}{\mathbf{U}}^{(k)}_{r}\right),\qquad i=1,\dots,k,
``` |  | (A.10) |

where $`\sigma_{i}(\cdot)`$ denotes the $`i`$-th singular value.

#### Maximum principal-angle rotation.

Max PA of the top-$`r`$ left singular vectors:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{maxPA}\left({\mathbf{W}}^{(0)},{\mathbf{W}}^{(k)}\right)=\max_{i\leq r}\theta_{i}({\mathbf{W}}^{(0)},{\mathbf{W}}^{(k)}).
``` |  | (A.11) |

#### Principal-mask overlap.

Intersection-over-Union between the initial and current PM masks:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{PMOverlap}\left({\mathbf{W}}^{(0)},{\mathbf{W}}^{(k)}\right)=\IoU\left({\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{principal}}}^{(0)},{\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{principal}}}^{(k)}\right).
``` |  | (A.12) |

#### Changed-parameter-mask.

Per-parameter mask with change threshold $`\eta>0`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
{\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{param}}}^{(k)}[i,j]=\mathbb{I}\left(\left|\left({\mathbf{W}}^{(k)}-{\mathbf{W}}^{(0)}\right)[i,j]\right|\geq\eta\right).
``` |  | (A.13) |

#### Principal-mask update sparsity.

Intersection-over-Union between the initial principal mask and the
changed-parameter mask:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{PMUpdateSparsity}\left({\mathbf{W}}^{(0)},{\mathbf{W}}^{(k)}\right)=\IoU{\left({\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{principal}}}^{(0)},{\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{param}}}^{(k)}\right)}.
``` |  | (A.14) |

## Appendix B Proofs

We provide the proofs for results in
[Section 5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Theoretical View on Forgetting: Excess KL Drift ‣ 5 Understanding SDPO in Continual Post-training ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training").
All distributions are over finite spaces. We assume that the base
sequence distribution $`P_{0}(\cdot\mid x)`$ has full support. When the
prompt $`x`$ is fixed, we suppress it from notation.

#### Matched-success Razor policy.

Let $`S=S_{x}`$ be the set of successful responses and let
$`z=P_{0}(S\mid x)\in(0,1)`$. For a target success level
$`\alpha\in(0,1)`$, define

|     |                                                               |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathcal{Q}_{\alpha}=\{Q\in\Delta(\mathcal{Y}):Q(S)=\alpha\}.
       ```                                                            |     |

###### Lemma 2 (Closed form of the matched-success Razor policy).

The solution of

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
Q_{\alpha,x}^{\dagger}=\arg\min_{Q\in\mathcal{Q}_{\alpha}}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl(Q\parallel P_{0}(\cdot\mid x)\bigr)
``` |  |

is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
Q_{\alpha,x}^{\dagger}(y)=P_{0}(y\mid x)\left[\frac{\alpha}{z}\mathbf{1}\{y\in S_{x}\}+\frac{1-\alpha}{1-z}\mathbf{1}\{y\notin S_{x}\}\right].
``` |  | (B.1) |

Equivalently,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
Q_{\alpha,x}^{\dagger}=\alpha P_{0}(\cdot\mid x,S_{x})+(1-\alpha)P_{0}(\cdot\mid x,S_{x}^{c}).
``` |  |

###### Proof.

Fix $`x`$ and write $`p=P_{0}(\cdot\mid x)`$. Let
$`p^{+}=p(\cdot\mid S)`$ and $`p^{-}=p(\cdot\mid S^{c})`$. Any
$`Q\in\mathcal{Q}_{\alpha}`$ can be decomposed as

|     |                                 |     |
|-----|---------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       Q=\alpha Q^{+}+(1-\alpha)Q^{-},
       ```                              |     |

where $`Q^{+}=Q(\cdot\mid S)`$ and $`Q^{-}=Q(\cdot\mid S^{c})`$. Then

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\parallel p)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\alpha\log\frac{\alpha}{z}+(1-\alpha)\log\frac{1-\alpha}{1-z}+\alpha D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q^{+}\parallel p^{+})+(1-\alpha)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q^{-}\parallel p^{-}).`$ |  |

The first two terms are constant over $`\mathcal{Q}_{\alpha}`$. The
remaining terms are nonnegative and vanish if and only if
$`Q^{+}=p^{+}`$ and $`Q^{-}=p^{-}`$. Thus the unique minimizer is

|     |                                                      |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       Q_{\alpha,x}^{\dagger}=\alpha p^{+}+(1-\alpha)p^{-},
       ```                                                   |     |

which is exactly
[Equation B.1](#A2.E1 "In Lemma 2 (Closed form of the matched-success Razor policy). ‣ Matched-success Razor policy. ‣ Appendix B Proofs ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training").
∎

###### Lemma 3 (Token kernel induced by the Razor policy).

Let $`q_{\alpha,x}^{\dagger}(\cdot\mid h_{t})`$ be the autoregressive
token kernel induced by $`Q_{\alpha,x}^{\dagger}`$ at history
$`h_{t}=(x,y_{<t})`$. Define

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
C_{\alpha}(h)=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim P_{0}(\cdot\mid h)}\left[\frac{\alpha}{z}\mathbf{1}\{y\in S_{x}\}+\frac{1-\alpha}{1-z}\mathbf{1}\{y\notin S_{x}\}\right].
``` |  | (B.2) |

Then

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q_{\alpha,x}^{\dagger}(a\mid h_{t})=\pi_{0}(a\mid h_{t})\frac{C_{\alpha}(h_{t}a)}{C_{\alpha}(h_{t})}.
``` |  | (B.3) |

In the exact-success limit $`\alpha\to 1`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q_{1,x}^{\dagger}(a\mid h_{t})=\pi_{0}(a\mid h_{t})\frac{\Pr_{P_{0}}(y\in S_{x}\mid h_{t}a)}{\Pr_{P_{0}}(y\in S_{x}\mid h_{t})}.
``` |  | (B.4) |

###### Proof.

By
[Lemma 2](#Thmtheorem2 "Lemma 2 (Closed form of the matched-success Razor policy). ‣ Matched-success Razor policy. ‣ Appendix B Proofs ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training"),

|     |                                                        |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       Q_{\alpha,x}^{\dagger}(y)=P_{0}(y\mid x)w_{\alpha}(y),
       ```                                                     |     |

where

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
w_{\alpha}(y)=\frac{\alpha}{z}\mathbf{1}\{y\in S_{x}\}+\frac{1-\alpha}{1-z}\mathbf{1}\{y\notin S_{x}\}.
``` |  |

For a history $`h_{t}=(x,y_{<t})`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle q_{\alpha,x}^{\dagger}(a\mid h_{t})`$ | $`\displaystyle=\Pr_{Q_{\alpha,x}^{\dagger}}(y_{t}=a\mid h_{t})=\frac{\sum_{y_{>t}}P_{0}(a,y_{>t}\mid h_{t})w_{\alpha}(y)}{\sum_{\tilde{y}_{\geq t}}P_{0}(\tilde{y}_{\geq t}\mid h_{t})w_{\alpha}(\tilde{y})}.`$ |  |

The numerator equals

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\pi_{0}(a\mid h_{t})\mathbb{E}_{y\sim P_{0}(\cdot\mid h_{t}a)}[w_{\alpha}(y)]=\pi_{0}(a\mid h_{t})C_{\alpha}(h_{t}a),
``` |  |

and the denominator equals $`C_{\alpha}(h_{t})`$. This proves
[Equation B.3](#A2.E3 "In Lemma 3 (Token kernel induced by the Razor policy). ‣ Matched-success Razor policy. ‣ Appendix B Proofs ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training").
Letting $`\alpha\to 1`$ gives
[Equation B.4](#A2.E4 "In Lemma 3 (Token kernel induced by the Razor policy). ‣ Matched-success Razor policy. ‣ Appendix B Proofs ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training").
∎

#### Teacher projection and excess reverse KL.

For a strict distillation divergence $`D`$, the population SDPO token
target is

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
B(\cdot\mid h_{t})\in\arg\min_{u\in\Delta(\mathcal{V})}\mathbb{E}_{c\mid h_{t}}D\bigl(u,T_{c}(\cdot\mid h_{t})\bigr).
``` |  |

When $`c`$ is deterministic and $`D`$ is generalized JSD, the minimizer
is $`B(\cdot\mid h_{t})=T_{c}(\cdot\mid h_{t})`$ because generalized JSD
is nonnegative and equals zero if and only if its two arguments are
identical.

Let $`P_{B}(\cdot\mid x)`$ be the sequence distribution induced by
$`B(\cdot\mid h_{t})`$, and let

|     |                            |     |
|-----|----------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \alpha=P_{B}(S_{x}\mid x).
       ```                         |     |

The corresponding matched-success Razor policy is
$`Q_{\alpha,x}^{\dagger}`$.

###### Proof of [Theorem 1](#Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 1 (Teacher projection induces excess KL drift). ‣ 5.3 Theoretical View on Forgetting: Excess KL Drift ‣ 5 Understanding SDPO in Continual Post-training ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training").

Fix $`x`$ and suppress $`x`$ from notation. Let
$`p=P_{0}(\cdot\mid x)`$, $`S=S_{x}`$, $`z=p(S)`$, and
$`Q^{\dagger}=Q_{\alpha,x}^{\dagger}`$. By
[Lemma 2](#Thmtheorem2 "Lemma 2 (Closed form of the matched-success Razor policy). ‣ Matched-success Razor policy. ‣ Appendix B Proofs ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training"),

|     |                                   |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       Q^{\dagger}(y)=p(y)w_{\alpha}(y),
       ```                                |     |

where $`w_{\alpha}(y)=\alpha/z`$ on $`S`$ and
$`w_{\alpha}(y)=(1-\alpha)/(1-z)`$ on $`S^{c}`$.

Since $`P_{B}(S)=Q^{\dagger}(S)=\alpha`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\sum_{y}P_{B}(y)\log w_{\alpha}(y)=\sum_{y}Q^{\dagger}(y)\log w_{\alpha}(y).
``` |  | (B.5) |

Therefore,

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{B}\parallel p)-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q^{\dagger}\parallel p)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{y}P_{B}(y)\log\frac{P_{B}(y)}{p(y)}-\sum_{y}Q^{\dagger}(y)\log\frac{Q^{\dagger}(y)}{p(y)}`$ |  | (B.6) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{y}P_{B}(y)\log\frac{P_{B}(y)}{p(y)}-\sum_{y}Q^{\dagger}(y)\log w_{\alpha}(y)`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{y}P_{B}(y)\log\frac{P_{B}(y)}{p(y)w_{\alpha}(y)}`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{B}\parallel Q^{\dagger}),`$ |  |  |

where we used
[Equation B.5](#A2.E5 "In Proof of . ‣ Teacher projection and excess reverse KL. ‣ Appendix B Proofs ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")
in the third line.

Now write both sequence distributions autoregressively:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
P_{B}(y\mid x)=\prod_{t=1}^{H}B(y_{t}\mid h_{t}),\qquad Q^{\dagger}(y\mid x)=\prod_{t=1}^{H}q_{\alpha,x}^{\dagger}(y_{t}\mid h_{t}).
``` |  |

Then the autoregressive KL chain rule gives

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{B}\parallel Q^{\dagger})`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim P_{B}}\log\frac{P_{B}(y\mid x)}{Q^{\dagger}(y\mid x)}`$ |  | (B.7) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim P_{B}}\sum_{t=1}^{H}\log\frac{B(y_{t}\mid h_{t})}{q_{\alpha,x}^{\dagger}(y_{t}\mid h_{t})}`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim P_{B}}\sum_{t=1}^{H}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl(B(\cdot\mid h_{t})\parallel q_{\alpha,x}^{\dagger}(\cdot\mid h_{t})\bigr).`$ |  |  |

Combining
[Equation B.6](#A2.E6 "In Proof of . ‣ Teacher projection and excess reverse KL. ‣ Appendix B Proofs ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")
and
[Equation B.7](#A2.E7 "In Proof of . ‣ Teacher projection and excess reverse KL. ‣ Appendix B Proofs ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")
proves the theorem. The right-hand side is nonnegative, and it is
strictly positive whenever the two token kernels differ on a set of
histories with positive $`P_{B}`$-probability. ∎

#### Forward KL counterpart.

The previous theorem uses reverse KL because RL’s Razor is naturally
stated as a reverse-KL projection. The empirical forgetting law is often
measured by forward KL from the base policy to the fine-tuned policy, so
we also give the matched-success forward-KL analogue.

###### Proposition 4 (Forward-KL excess at matched success).

Fix $`x`$ and let $`p=P_{0}(\cdot\mid x)`$. Let $`S=S_{x}`$, $`z=p(S)`$,
and let $`P_{B}(S)=\alpha\in(0,1)`$. Define

|     |                                                       |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       p^{+}=p(\cdot\mid S),\qquad p^{-}=p(\cdot\mid S^{c}),
       ```                                                    |     |

and

|     |                                                               |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       B^{+}=P_{B}(\cdot\mid S),\qquad B^{-}=P_{B}(\cdot\mid S^{c}).
       ```                                                            |     |

Then

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\parallel P_{B})-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\parallel Q_{\alpha,x}^{\dagger})=zD_{\mathrm{KL}}(p^{+}\parallel B^{+})+(1-z)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p^{-}\parallel B^{-})\geq 0.`$ |  | (B.8) |

###### Proof.

Decompose $`P_{B}`$ as

|     |                                     |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       P_{B}=\alpha B^{+}+(1-\alpha)B^{-}.
       ```                                  |     |

Then

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\parallel P_{B})`$ | $`\displaystyle=z\log\frac{z}{\alpha}+(1-z)\log\frac{1-z}{1-\alpha}+zD_{\mathrm{KL}}(p^{+}\parallel B^{+})+(1-z)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p^{-}\parallel B^{-}).`$ |  |

For $`Q_{\alpha,x}^{\dagger}=\alpha p^{+}+(1-\alpha)p^{-}`$, the two
conditional KL terms vanish:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\parallel Q_{\alpha,x}^{\dagger})=z\log\frac{z}{\alpha}+(1-z)\log\frac{1-z}{1-\alpha}.
``` |  |

Subtracting gives
[Equation B.8](#A2.E8 "In Proposition 4 (Forward-KL excess at matched success). ‣ Forward KL counterpart. ‣ Appendix B Proofs ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training").
∎

#### Connection to forgetting.

We use the KL-forgetting law as an empirical bridge between
distributional drift and prior-task forgetting.

###### Assumption 5 (KL-forgetting law).

For policies matched in new-task success, let $`\mathsf{F}(\pi)`$ denote
the drop in prior-task performance. Suppose there exists a strictly
increasing function $`\omega`$ with $`\omega(0)=0`$ such that

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{fwd}}(\pi_{1})-\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{fwd}}(\pi_{2})\geq\varepsilon\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathsf{F}(\pi_{1})-\mathsf{F}(\pi_{2})\geq\omega(\varepsilon),
``` |  |

where

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{fwd}}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl(P_{0}(\cdot\mid x)\parallel P_{\pi}(\cdot\mid x)\bigr).
``` |  |

###### Corollary 6 (Teacher mismatch implies additional forgetting).

Let $`P_{B}`$ be the SDPO teacher-projected sequence distribution and
let $`Q_{\alpha,x}^{\dagger}`$ be the matched-success Razor policy with
$`\alpha=P_{B}(S_{x}\mid x)`$. Define

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\Delta_{\mathrm{fwd}}=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\Bigl[`$ | $`\displaystyle z_{x}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl(P_{0}(\cdot\mid x,S_{x})\parallel P_{B}(\cdot\mid x,S_{x})\bigr)`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle+(1-z_{x})D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl(P_{0}(\cdot\mid x,S_{x}^{c})\parallel P_{B}(\cdot\mid x,S_{x}^{c})\bigr)\Bigr].`$ |  |

If $`\Delta_{\mathrm{fwd}}>0`$, then under
[Assumption 5](#Thmtheorem5 "Assumption 5 (KL-forgetting law). ‣ Connection to forgetting. ‣ Appendix B Proofs ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training"),

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathsf{F}(P_{B})-\mathsf{F}(Q_{\alpha}^{\dagger})\geq\omega(\Delta_{\mathrm{fwd}})>0.
``` |  |

###### Proof.

Taking expectation over $`x\sim\mathcal{D}`$ in
[Proposition 4](#Thmtheorem4 "Proposition 4 (Forward-KL excess at matched success). ‣ Forward KL counterpart. ‣ Appendix B Proofs ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training")
gives

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{fwd}}(P_{B})-\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{fwd}}(Q_{\alpha}^{\dagger})=\Delta_{\mathrm{fwd}}.
``` |  |

The result follows directly from
[Assumption 5](#Thmtheorem5 "Assumption 5 (KL-forgetting law). ‣ Connection to forgetting. ‣ Appendix B Proofs ‣ Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training").
∎
````
